embezzle

/em-BEZ-ul/ — rhymes with nuzzle · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To embezzle money is to secretly steal funds that were entrusted to your care, usually at a job.

The treasurer embezzled club funds by writing checks to a fake company.

Example

A bank manager embezzles millions from customer accounts, moving the money into secret overseas accounts and making the transfers look legitimate to cover her tracks.

Embezzle captures the core violation—she was entrusted with access and secretly violated that trust. Plain 'steal' would miss the crucial ingredient: the position of trust she held.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

steal: To steal is simply to take what does not belong to you — any thief can steal, whether a stranger's bike or cash from a till. To embezzle is a special kind of stealing: quietly draining money that was entrusted to your care, usually at a job.

defraud: To defraud someone is to cheat them out of money through dishonesty, and the cheat can be a total stranger — you defraud the victim, a person or a company. To embezzle, you must first be trusted: it is the insider's crime of stealing funds placed in your care.

misappropriate: To misappropriate money is to use funds entrusted to you wrongly — even openly or carelessly, like spending grant money on the wrong project. To embezzle is narrower and darker: secretly stealing entrusted money for yourself and hiding the theft behind false records.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

restore: to give back what was taken

repay: to return money that is owed

Where it sits · how dishonest and planned the theft is

borrow → take → pocket → embezzle

borrow vs. embezzle: Borrow is the innocent bottom of this scale, nothing like embezzle: borrowing means taking with permission and giving back, while embezzling is the secret theft of money placed in your care.

take vs. embezzle: Take is far weaker than embezzle — taking something can be casual or even completely honest, but to embezzle is to deliberately and secretly steal funds that were entrusted to you.

pocket vs. embezzle: Pocket is sneaky but small-scale next to embezzle: pocketing some loose cash is petty theft of the moment, while embezzling is a calculated, ongoing scheme to drain entrusted money.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — em-: in, into (here strengthening the verb) (Old French (en-))

Root — bezzle: to plunder, destroy, make disappear (Old French (besillier), ultimate origin unknown)

Put it together: The prefix em- intensifies an old French verb besillier, meaning 'to plunder or make disappear' — so embezzle grew from the idea of making someone else's property vanish, which is still exactly what an embezzler does with entrusted funds.

Use the root in a new word: embezzlement: The accountant was charged with embezzlement — the crime of embezzling — showing how the same rare root builds the official name of the offense itself.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / financial

Embezzle is a legal and financial term—reach for it when fraud involves stolen funds, not just any theft. It implies a special position of trust and access. For a simple robbery, use 'steal' or 'rob'.
